hero.name: Ritu
hero.who: a staff nurse in Lucknow on rotating shifts whose big resolutions keep collapsing

story.b: On the first of January, Ritu taped a list to her cupboard. One hour of yoga daily, eight glasses of water, no fried food, twenty pages of reading before bed. She is a staff nurse at a hospital in Lucknow, and her shifts rotate every week. The night-shift week ended the yoga by day four. Her water bottle sits full in her locker after twelve-hour shifts. By February the list is curling at the corners, and she has stopped looking at it. Her younger brother Rohit jokes that she gives injections to strangers but cannot keep one promise to herself. She laughs, then feels worse. She starts to believe she simply has no willpower.

ask.q: Ritu has dropped every big resolution and now thinks she has no willpower. What should she do next?
o: Write a stricter list and punish herself for each miss
Give up on habits until her shifts become regular
Pick one habit and make it so small it fits even a night shift
ask.why: Her failures come from plans that need a good day, and a rotating shift guarantees bad ones. A tiny habit survives any shift. Stricter rules and self-punishment add guilt, not ability, and waiting for regular shifts could mean waiting forever. Design beats willpower.

chapters.take: When habits collapse, blame the design, not your character.

story.h: Three words on a sticky note
story.b: During a quiet night shift, Ritu thinks about the water bottle. She wants to drink more, because the headaches after shifts are awful. Drinking water is easy. So what broke? Nothing ever reminds her. The bottle sits in a locker two corridors away, and she only remembers it when the headache starts. She writes three words on a sticky note: want, easy, reminder. Her want is strong. Ease is a problem, because the bottle is far. The reminder is missing completely. On the next shift she clips a small bottle to the medicine trolley she pushes every hour. By morning it is empty, and for once she gets home without a pounding head.

ask.q: Her colleague Shabnam badly wants to study for an exam and keeps the book in her bag, yet never opens it. What is most likely missing?
o: A prompt that reminds her at the right moment to open the book
Enough motivation, so she should watch inspiring videos
Talent, so she should accept the exam is not for her
ask.why: Shabnam already wants it and the book is right there, so motivation and ability are in place. What is missing is a reminder at the right moment. More inspiration adds nothing she lacks, and blaming talent ignores the simple gap. Find which piece broke, then fix that one.

chapters.take: Every action needs motivation, ability and a prompt. Find the missing one.

story.b: Ritu still wants yoga in her life. Her back aches from lifting patients, and she misses how light she felt in college. But the one-hour plan needed a motivated Ritu, and that Ritu shows up maybe twice a month. So she asks a different question. What could she do even after the worst night shift? The answer is almost embarrassing. One slow stretch on the floor beside her bed. That is the whole habit. Some mornings she does one and crawls into bed. Some mornings she feels good and does ten minutes. Either way it counts. After a brutal week with two emergencies, she notices the stretch is the only plan that survived.

ask.q: Her brother Rohit wants to start running and plans five kilometres a day from Monday. What would Ritu advise?
o: Wait for a day when he feels really fired up to begin
Start with just putting on his shoes and walking to the gate
Run ten kilometres on day one to prove he is serious
ask.why: Motivation rises and falls, so a habit that needs a big push dies on the first tired day. Putting on shoes and reaching the gate is easy enough for his worst mood. Waiting for inspiration delays the start, and a huge first run usually ends in soreness and quitting.

chapters.take: Make it so easy you can do it on your worst day.

story.b: Ritu used to read every night as a girl. Now novels pile up on her windowsill, untouched. Her shifts change every week, so a fixed time like ten at night never works. But one thing happens after every single shift, day or night. She comes home and hangs her uniform on the hook behind the door. So she writes a small recipe on a card. After I hang my uniform on the hook, I will read one page. She keeps the novel on the shelf right beside the hook. The first week she reads one page standing up. By the third week she sometimes sits on the floor, still in her socks, and reads a whole chapter.

ask.q: Ritu also wants to message her grandmother daily, but she keeps forgetting. Which plan fits best?
o: Set a fixed alarm at nine every evening, whatever her shift
Promise herself she will remember whenever she has a free moment
Send the message right after she parks her scooter at home each day
ask.why: Parking her scooter happens after every shift, so it is a reliable prompt that moves with her schedule. A nine o'clock alarm will ring in the middle of night duty, and vague promises to remember are exactly what has failed. Tie the new habit to something she already does.

chapters.take: After something you already do daily, add the tiny new habit.

story.b: The page-a-day habit is working, but the stretch still feels like a chore. Ritu decides to try something that feels a bit silly. Right after her one stretch, she smiles and whispers yes to herself, the way she does when a difficult cannula goes in on the first try. The first few times she feels foolish. Her roommate catches her once and laughs. But within a couple of weeks, Ritu notices she looks forward to the stretch. The little burst of feeling good has become part of it. She starts doing the same after every tiny habit, a quick yes or a small fist pump, and each one feels a little more like her own.

ask.q: Ritu's roommate starts a tiny habit but feels nothing about it and soon drifts away. What would help the habit stick?
o: Celebrate right after doing it, with a smile or a quick yes
Do it more times a day, so repetition alone wires it in
Scold herself whenever she skips it, so she fears missing
ask.why: Habits seem to wire in faster when a good feeling follows the action right away. A quick celebration gives that feeling. Repetition without any feeling is slower and duller, and scolding links the habit with bad feelings, which makes her want to avoid it.

chapters.take: A tiny celebration right after a habit helps it stick.

story.b: Ritu's tiny habits are growing on their own. The one stretch is now often fifteen minutes. The single page often becomes a chapter. But one habit she wants gone is the packet of chips she buys every night shift at three in the morning. The vending machine glows right beside the lift she takes on every round. Fighting it with willpower at that hour has never worked. So she changes the setup. She uses the stairs instead of the lift on her rounds. She leaves her coins in the locker. And she packs a small box of roasted chana in her pocket for when real hunger comes.

ask.q: Rohit scrolls his phone in bed for an hour every night and hates it. What should he try first?
o: Promise to scroll for only five minutes and trust himself
Charge the phone outside the bedroom and keep a book by the bed
Delete every app at once and hope the urge disappears
ask.why: An unwanted habit is easier to change by removing its prompt and making it harder than by fighting it in the moment. Charging the phone outside does both, and the book is a better swap. A five-minute promise needs willpower at the weakest time, and deleting everything often ends in reinstalling it all.

chapters.take: Let good habits grow gently, and make unwanted ones harder to reach.

story.h: A card instead of a list
story.b: By May, the old New Year list is gone from the cupboard. In its place is a small card with three lines. After I hang my uniform, one page. After I wake, one stretch. After I park my scooter, one message to Dadi. Most days Ritu does more than the card asks, and on bad days she does exactly what it says. She has finished four novels. Her back feels better after long shifts. Her grandmother now waits for the message and replies with voice notes. When a junior nurse confesses that she keeps failing her resolutions, Ritu does not lecture. She asks what the smallest possible version would be, and what daily routine it could follow.

chapters.take: Tiny habits, kept kindly, quietly become a different life.
